subject: Logistic Regression with low success probability

messages.author: 142bbec126d79068
messages.subject: Logistic Regression with low success probability
parts:
Hello all,

Apologies upfront if this issue has been addressed but I could not find it mentioned. I'm dealing with a situation where I want to run logistic regression with INLA with a fake clinical trial data set. My fake data set consists of 50 "control" and 50 "treat" (x = 0 or 1) with both groups having a success probability of 0.02 or 0.01.

My method is this, simulate 100 response values from rbernoulli(n = 1, p =  0.02), run this with INLA with the default priors, and get the posterior P(\beta_1 > 0 | data). I'm doing this to do a version of a power calculation but to do so I need to run the null case first, hence why I have both groups with the same success probability.

The posterior probability that \beta_1 > 0 should be centered at 0.5 since both groups have the same success probability but when I repeat this simulation 50-100 times I have generally been seeing that the posterior probabilities are skewed lower. For example, in cases where there were no drawn successes (y_i = 0 for all i) the posterior probability was sometimes as low as 0.12.

Also strange is that the parameter estimate for \beta_1 is often very different from the frequentist estimate (sometimes a difference of 10 or more). I assume these problems are because the success probability is so low but I was wondering if anyone else has run into this issue and if they had any solutions. 

I tried weakly informative priors on the intercept and \beta_1 parameter but that did not seem to help much. Centering the x values about 0 helped the parameter estimate slightly but the posterior probabilities were still skewed (x = -0.5 or x = 0.5). Below is some relevant code that I've been looping through to get the posterior probabilities and parameter estimates. Thanks in advance!

# success probs
null_p <- 0.02
alt_p <- 0.02

# control or treat
x <- 
    rep(c(0, 1), each = 50) %>%
    sample()

n <- length(x)

# overkill step for this context since null_p = alt_p 
# sets p = 0.02 for all cases 
p_assign <-
    tibble(x = treat_vec) %>%
    mutate(p = case_when(
      x == 1 ~ alt_p,
      x == 0 ~ null_p
    ))

# tibble to store response
  response <- tibble(y = numeric())
 

# looping here in case null_p ever not the same as alt_p
# draw y's using p's calculated above
  for (i in 1:n) {
    new_y <- tibble(y = rbernoulli(n = 1, p = p_assign$p[i]))
    response <- bind_rows(response, new_y)
  }
 

# bind x's and y's
dat <-
    tibble(x = treat_vec, y = response$y)

# optional prior 
# -3.89 is beta_0 when p = 0.02 and x = 0
#priors <- list(mean.intercept = -3.89, prec.intercept = 0.01,
#                 mean = list(x = 0), prec = list(x= 0.04))

# run INLA
mod_full <- inla(y ~ x,  data = dat, family = "binomial", Ntrials = 1,
                  control.family = list(link = "logit"))
                 # , control.fixed = priors)

# freq logistic
mod_freq_full <-
    glm(y ~ x, data = dat, family = "binomial")

# estimates
inla_est_full <- mod_full$summary.fixed$mean[2]
freq_est_full <- as.numeric(mod_freq_full$coefficients['x'])

# grab marginal for \beta_1
marg_x_full <- mod_full$marginals.fixed$x

# 1 - pdf gives P(\beta_1 > 0 | data)
prob_0_full <- 1 - inla.pmarginal(0, marg_x_full)
